## Overview

The main analysis estimates geographic heterogeneity in both child mortality risk and the absolute effect of biannual azithromycin distribution across Niger's Dosso region. A programme question follows directly: **if you cannot treat everywhere, does prioritising places by mortality recover most of the benefit of prioritising by treatment effect?**

We quantify how closely mortality-based prioritisation tracks effect-based prioritisation, at the village, CSI and department scales. We're not saying that baseline mortality determines effect magnitude, but that shared upstream factors, (such as access to care) drive both surfaces.

Every figure and table below is computed under **two treatment-by-space specifications from 02A** — the linear interaction (primary) and the spline interaction — rather than one, because how much of the mortality/effect agreement is structural rather than empirical is exactly what changes between them. Inline numbers in the prose are quoted for one reference specification, named each time; the figures carry the comparison.

### Setup

1.  "Baseline" mortality is $\hat\mu^0_i$, the predicted *control-arm* mortality rate in village $i$, in deaths per 1000 child-years — not observed pre-treatment mortality. The control group pools AVENIR's placebo and infant-azithromycin arms.
2.  The predicted effect is $\widehat{RD}_i = \hat\mu^0_i - \hat\mu^1_i$, the rate difference between the two arms at village $i$, on the same deaths-per-1000-child-years scale. It is signed so that **positive means benefit**: $\widehat{RD}_i > 0$ is deaths averted by treating, $\widehat{RD}_i < 0$ is predicted harm. Note the sign convention is the negative of the ATE ($\hat\mu^1 - \hat\mu^0$) reported elsewhere in this repo.
3.  $\hat\mu^0_i$ and $\widehat{RD}_i$ come from the same fit, evaluated at the villages whose own outcomes informed it. How much of the agreement between the two rankings is induced by the model rather than by the data depends on the specification — which is why both are run side by side here rather than one being chosen.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

rm(list = ls())

```{r packages and paths}

# Unlike earlier versions of this document, 07 is no longer standalone: the
# package attachments, the geospatial parameters (global_crs, proj_crs), the
# figure path and the rebuild flags all come from 0-config.R, and the raster
# helpers from 0-functions.R, rather than being redeclared here.
source(here::here("analysis", "0-config.R"))
source(here::here("analysis", "0-functions.R"))
source(here::here("analysis", "07x-functions.R"))

# 0-config.R deliberately does NOT attach spaMM (the rest of the repo calls
# spaMM::fitme() namespaced). It has to be attached here: the fitted objects are
# read back with readRDS(), and a bare predict() on an HLfit object dispatches
# to predict.default() unless spaMM's methods are registered.
library(spaMM)

# Note: the three prediction inputs read below are built by `07x-data_prep.R`,
# which is not part of run-all.R. Run it once before rendering this document.
#
# No set.seed() here, and the document is fully deterministic: every number is a
# functional of the fitted surface, with no simulation step. The `random` rule is
# the 45-degree line by construction, not by simulation.

# Protection conferred by one AVENIR distribution round, in years, assumed
# common across rounds. The Data section checks the assumption against observed
# follow-up: total doses x phase_years should reproduce the child-years the
# trial actually accrued.
phase_years <- 0.5

# Shared x-grid for every targeting curve, on the proportion-of-doses scale.
# Fixed rather than at observed knots so all rules share one grid.
x_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.005)

# Coverage levels reported in the tables below.
coverage_marks <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 0.75)

# Pull the grid point nearest a target coverage. Matching on == would work for
# the current grid but silently return nothing if x_grid's step changes, which
# would empty a table or an inline number without any error.
nearest_x <- function(target) x_grid[which.min(abs(x_grid - target))]
```

```{r models}

# The three treatment-by-space specifications from 02A. gen_krig_int comes
# first because it is the reference specification the prose quotes and the one
# the cumulative heat map below is built for; the facet order follows this
# vector everywhere.
model_names <- c("fitmort_child_gen_krig_int",
                 # "fitmort_child_doub_matern",
                 "fitmort_child_gen_krig_spline")

# Short keys, as used by preds_ATE.rds and by the lookup tables below. The
# fitted objects in data/ prefix them with "fitmort_child_".
model_keys <- sub("^fitmort_child_", "", model_names)

# Human-readable names, per the manuscript's model table.
model_display <- c(
  simp_krig       = "Baseline spatial model",
  gen_krig        = "Spatial trend model",
  gen_krig_int    = "Spatially heterogeneous ATE model",
  doub_matern     = "Matern treatment interaction model",
  gen_krig_spline = "Spline treatment interaction model"
)

if (!all(model_keys %in% names(model_display))) {
  stop("No display name on file for: ",
       paste(setdiff(model_keys, names(model_display)), collapse = ", "),
       ". Add one to `model_display`.")
}

# Reference specification for every inline number in the prose, and the single
# model the cumulative deaths-averted heat map is drawn for. Named explicitly
# wherever it is quoted, so no number in the text is unattributed.
ref_key     <- "gen_krig_int"
ref_model   <- paste0("fitmort_child_", ref_key)
ref_display <- model_display[[ref_key]]

stopifnot(ref_key %in% model_keys)

# Facet order and labels. Defined once here because eight figures below share
# them, and a facet whose order drifted between figures would invite reading
# two panels in different positions as the same model.
model_levels <- unname(model_display[model_keys])

as_model_label <- function(key) {
  factor(unname(model_display[key]), levels = model_levels)
}
```

### Data

```{r read inputs}

grappe_dat <- readRDS(here("data", "grappe_mortality_data.rds"))
phase_dat  <- readRDS(here("data", "grappe_mortality_data_by_phase.rds"))
dose_dat   <- readRDS(here("data", "grappe_dose_counts_by_phase.rds"))
```

```{r build prediction tables}

# The prediction table is the single object every function in `07x-functions.R`
# consumes. Building it once per model and caching each as `.rds` keeps the table
# - rather than the model - as the interface, which is what lets the multi-model
# comparison be layered on without touching any function body.
#
# The cache is not keyed on its inputs. Stamping the settings onto the saved
# table and checking them on load is what stops a later edit to phase_years,
# either CRS, or the model list from silently leaving every number in this
# document computed under the old settings. `exposure` is part of the stamp so a
# table built under the earlier doses-delivered benefit denominator cannot be
# reused now that deaths averted use observed person-time (the curve's x-axis
# budget is doses; the benefit exposure is person-time).
pred_params_for <- function(this_model) {
  list(model       = this_model,
       exposure    = "observed_person_time",
       phase_years = phase_years,
       global_crs  = global_crs,
       proj_crs    = proj_crs)
}

pred_tables <- purrr::map(model_names, function(this_model) {

  pred_path   <- here("data", paste0("targeting_prediction_table_", this_model, ".rds"))
  pred_params <- pred_params_for(this_model)

  if (rebuild_targeting_preds_flag || !file.exists(pred_path)) {

    spamm_fit <- readRDS(here("data", paste0(this_model, ".rds")))

    pred_table <- build_prediction_table(
      spamm_model_fit = spamm_fit,
      grappe_dat      = grappe_dat,
      phase_dat       = phase_dat,
      dose_dat        = dose_dat,
      phase_years     = phase_years,
      global_crs      = global_crs,
      proj_crs        = proj_crs
    )

    attr(pred_table, "pred_params") <- pred_params
    saveRDS(pred_table, pred_path)

    pred_table

  } else {

    pred_table <- readRDS(pred_path)

    if (!identical(attr(pred_table, "pred_params"), pred_params)) {
      stop("The cached prediction table at ", pred_path, " was built under ",
           "different settings than the ones declared above. Set ",
           "rebuild_targeting_preds_flag <- TRUE in 0-config.R.")
    }

    pred_table
  }
}) %>%
  setNames(model_keys)

# Reference-model shorthands. Every quantity in the Data section that does not
# depend on the specification (doses, coverage, crude rates) is identical across
# the three tables; the ones that do are reported for both in the surface
# table below.
pred_table <- pred_tables[[ref_key]]
pred_dept  <- aggregate_predictions(pred_table, level = "department")
```


```{r descriptives}

n_grappes <- nrow(pred_table)
n_csi     <- dplyr::n_distinct(pred_table$csi)
n_dept    <- dplyr::n_distinct(pred_table$district)

grappes_per_csi <- pred_table %>% count(csi) %>% pull(n)
dose_share_dept <- pred_dept %>%
  mutate(share = 100 * n_doses / sum(n_doses)) %>%
  arrange(share)

# unname() throughout: quantile() returns named values, which knitr would
# otherwise carry into the inline text.
total_doses  <- sum(pred_table$n_doses)
n_doses_med  <- median(pred_table$n_doses)
n_doses_q1   <- unname(quantile(pred_table$n_doses, 0.25))
n_doses_q3   <- unname(quantile(pred_table$n_doses, 0.75))

# Total observed child-years at risk across the analytic grappes, the benefit
# exposure that converts RD into deaths averted. Reported alongside the dose
# totals so both the x-axis budget (doses) and the benefit exposure (person-time)
# are on the record.
total_person_time <- sum(pred_table$person_time)
pt_med  <- median(pred_table$person_time)
pt_q1   <- unname(quantile(pred_table$person_time, 0.25))
pt_q3   <- unname(quantile(pred_table$person_time, 0.75))

# Coverage, computed round by round -----
#
# n_children is the sum of started_phase_1to59 over a grappe's phases, and
# started_phase_1to59 counts a child once per phase. It is therefore a child-
# *round* total on the same footing as n_doses, not a count of distinct
# children, and the ratio is coverage per round.
#
# Matching doses to children *within* a round is what separates a genuine
# delivery shortfall from a missing dose record. A grappe with no dose row for
# one of its four rounds would otherwise show ~75% coverage purely because the
# denominator still counts that round's children — an artefact of the record
# gap, not a delivery failure.
coverage_round <- phase_dat %>%
  dplyr::filter(site_code %in% pred_table$site_code) %>%
  dplyr::select(site_code, phase, n_children_round = started_phase_1to59) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(dose_dat %>% dplyr::select(site_code, phase, n_doses),
                   by = c("site_code", "phase"))

# Grappe-rounds that appear in the mortality data with no dose record. These
# contribute zero to N_i (the intended reading: no record = no distribution)
# but are excluded from the coverage denominator, since a data-entry gap and a
# genuine non-distribution are indistinguishable here.
gap_rows      <- is.na(coverage_round$n_doses)
n_round_gaps  <- sum(gap_rows)
n_grappe_gaps <- dplyr::n_distinct(coverage_round$site_code[gap_rows])

matched_rounds <- coverage_round %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(n_doses))

dose_coverage <- sum(matched_rounds$n_doses) / sum(matched_rounds$n_children_round)

cov_grappe <- matched_rounds %>%
  group_by(site_code) %>%
  summarise(cov = sum(n_doses) / sum(n_children_round), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pull(cov)

cov_med   <- median(cov_grappe)
cov_q1    <- unname(quantile(cov_grappe, 0.25))
cov_q3    <- unname(quantile(cov_grappe, 0.75))
cov_min   <- min(cov_grappe)
n_low_cov <- sum(cov_grappe < 0.8)

# Per-round dose counts, subset to the analytic grappes and reshaped for the
# boxplot below. Grappe-rounds with no dose record are absent rather than
# zero, so the by-round boxes describe rounds that happened.
dose_by_round <- dose_dat %>%
  dplyr::filter(site_code %in% pred_table$site_code) %>%
  mutate(phase = as.factor(phase))

# Crude arm-specific rates, as a reference point for the predicted surface
crude <- grappe_dat %>%
  group_by(isTreated_child) %>%
  summarise(rate = 1000 * sum(n_deaths_1to59) / sum(pt_year_1to59),
            .groups = "drop")
crude_ctrl <- crude$rate[crude$isTreated_child == "Control"]
crude_trt  <- crude$rate[crude$isTreated_child == "Treatment"]
crude_rd   <- crude_ctrl - crude_trt

# Predicted surface, one row per model. The person-time-weighted means are the
# like-for-like comparison with the crude rates above, which are themselves
# person-time ratios of pooled totals; the medians are quoted alongside because
# the surface is right-skewed and the two summaries differ by more than a
# rounding error.
surface_tab <- purrr::imap_dfr(pred_tables, function(dat, this_key) {
  tibble::tibble(
    model         = this_key,
    mu0_wmean     = stats::weighted.mean(dat$mu0, w = dat$person_time),
    mu0_med       = median(dat$mu0),
    mu0_p05       = unname(quantile(dat$mu0, 0.05)),
    mu0_p95       = unname(quantile(dat$mu0, 0.95)),
    rd_wmean      = stats::weighted.mean(dat$rd, w = dat$person_time),
    rd_med        = median(dat$rd),
    rd_p05        = unname(quantile(dat$rd, 0.05)),
    rd_p95        = unname(quantile(dat$rd, 0.95)),
    pct_rd_neg    = 100 * mean(dat$rd < 0),
    total_averted = sum(dat$deaths_averted))
})

surface_of <- function(column, key = ref_key) {
  surface_tab[[column]][surface_tab$model == key]
}

total_averted   <- surface_of("total_averted")
pct_rd_negative <- surface_of("pct_rd_neg")
```

<!-- The analytic sample is `r scales::comma(n_grappes)`^★^ grappes in `r n_csi`^★^ CSIs and `r n_dept`^★^ departments of Dosso region (median `r median(grappes_per_csi)`^★^ grappes per CSI, range `r min(grappes_per_csi)`–`r max(grappes_per_csi)`^★^). The departments are very unequal in size, from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(dose_share_dept$share))`%^★^ of all doses in `r dose_share_dept$unit_label[1]`^★^ to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(dose_share_dept$share))`%^★^ in `r dose_share_dept$unit_label[nrow(dose_share_dept)]`^★^ — which matters for the block rules, because a department-block rule moves `r sprintf("%.0f", max(dose_share_dept$share))`%^★^ of the region's doses in a single step. -->

**Person-time,** the benefit exposure. Each village contributes its observed child-years at risk, $\text{pt}_i$ (children 1–59 months): `r scales::comma(round(total_person_time))` child-years in total, median `r scales::comma(round(pt_med))` per village (IQR `r scales::comma(round(pt_q1))`–`r scales::comma(round(pt_q3))`). It converts the predicted rate difference into a count of deaths — deaths averted in village $i$ is $\widehat{RD}_i \cdot \text{pt}_i / 1000$ — and is the weight used to aggregate mortality to the CSI and department scales and in the rank concordance. It does not sit on the x-axis.

**Doses delivered,** $N_i$. $N_i$ is the number of azithro/placebo doses delivered to children 1–59 months, summed over distribution rounds by village: `r scales::comma(total_doses)` doses in total, median `r scales::comma(n_doses_med)` per village (IQR `r scales::comma(n_doses_q1)`–`r scales::comma(n_doses_q3)`). $N_i$ is the x-axis budget of the targeting curves: villages are added in each rule's rank order and the curve advances by each village's doses. It does not depend on the specification, so the same $N_i$ sits behind both sets of curves.

**Coverage.** Matching doses to children eligible at the beginning of each round, delivery covered `r scales::percent(dose_coverage, accuracy = 0.1)` of eligible child-rounds (per-village median `r scales::percent(cov_med, accuracy = 0.1)`, IQR `r scales::percent(cov_q1, accuracy = 0.1)`–`r scales::percent(cov_q3, accuracy = 0.1)`, minimum `r scales::percent(cov_min, accuracy = 0.1)`; `r n_low_cov` village`r if (n_low_cov != 1) "s"` below 80%). `r n_round_gaps` village-rounds across `r n_grappe_gaps` villages appear in the mortality data with no matching dose record. Those rounds contribute zero doses to $N_i$.

```{r doses by round boxplot}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

# Two panels rather than five boxes on one axis: the cumulative totals sit
# about four times higher than any single round, and on a shared scale the
# four round boxes would be squashed into the bottom of the panel.
p_dose_round <- ggplot(dose_by_round, aes(x = phase, y = n_doses)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2, outlier.size = 0.6,
               fill = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Doses delivered per village",
       title = "By round") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_dose_cum <- ggplot(pred_table, aes(x = "All rounds", y = n_doses)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2, outlier.size = 0.6,
               fill = "#e84d60", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Cumulative") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

(p_dose_round | p_dose_cum) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(4, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Doses delivered to children 1-59 months, per village")
```

Round 1 sits a little below the later rounds; rounds 2–4 are close to each other. The cumulative panel is $N_i$, the per-village dose count the targeting curves below are budgeted on (the x-axis).

**Predicted mortality surfaces.** Predictions below come from these three fitted models:

```{r model equations}
#| results: asis
#| echo: false

# The equations are keyed on the model names so the document cannot describe one
# specification while predicting from another. Keys are the short names
# preds_ATE.rds uses.
model_eq <- c(
  gen_krig     = "\\log(\\mu_i) = \\log(PT_i) + \\beta_0 + \\beta_1 Trt_i + \\beta_2 lat_i + \\beta_3 lon_i + w(s_i)",
  gen_krig_int = "\\log(\\mu_i) = \\log(PT_i) + \\beta_0 + \\beta_1 Trt_i + \\beta_2 lat_i + \\beta_3 lon_i + \\beta_4 (Trt_i \\times lat_i) + \\beta_5 (Trt_i \\times lon_i) + w(s_i)",
  doub_matern  = "\\log(\\mu_i) = \\log(PT_i) + \\beta_0 + \\beta_1 Trt_i + \\beta_2 lat_i + \\beta_3 lon_i + \\beta_4 (Trt_i \\times lat_i) + \\beta_5 (Trt_i \\times lon_i) + w(s_i) + u(s_i)\\,Trt_i",
  dist_FE      = "\\log(\\mu_i) = \\log(PT_i) + \\beta_0 + \\beta_1 Trt_i + \\beta_2 lat_i + \\beta_3 lon_i + \\gamma_{d(i)} + w(s_i)",
  gen_krig_spline = "\\log(\\mu_i) = \\log(PT_i) + \\beta_0 + \\beta_1 Trt_i + s_{lat}(lat_i) + s_{lon}(lon_i) + Trt_i \\times [s_{lat}(lat_i) + s_{lon}(lon_i)] + w(s_i)"
)

model_note <- c(
  gen_krig     = "One Matern field $w(s_i)$, shared by both arms, and no treatment-by-space interaction: the fitted rate ratio between arms is constant across the region.",
  gen_krig_int = "One Matern field $w(s_i)$, shared by both arms. It therefore **cancels** in the arm contrast, leaving $\\log(\\hat\\mu^1_i/\\hat\\mu^0_i)$ a deterministic plane in location — so $\\widehat{RD}_i = \\hat\\mu^0_i \\times f(\\text{location}_i)$ exactly, with no component independent of baseline mortality.",
  doub_matern  = "**Two** Matern fields: $w(s_i)$ shared by both arms, plus $u(s_i)$ entering only in the treated arm. The second field does *not* cancel in the contrast, so the predicted effect carries spatial structure of its own rather than being a pure rescaling of baseline mortality.",
  dist_FE      = "One Matern field $w(s_i)$ plus district fixed effects $\\gamma_{d(i)}$.",
  gen_krig_spline = "Natural cubic splines (4 df per axis) replace the linear lat/lon terms in both the baseline surface and the treatment interaction, so both may curve. The single Matern field is still shared by both arms and still **cancels** in the arm contrast."
)

# Longer form of the same structural point, used in the concordance caveat and
# in the Conclusions. Kept beside model_note so the two cannot disagree, and
# emitted inline rather than hard-written into the prose, because whether the
# Matern field cancels in the arm contrast is exactly what changes between
# specifications — and is the reason all three are shown.
model_struct <- c(
  gen_krig     = "This specification has no treatment-by-space term at all, so the fitted rate ratio between arms is constant and $\\widehat{RD}_i \\propto \\hat\\mu^0_i$ exactly. Every concordance below is 1 by construction and carries no information about targeting.",
  gen_krig_int = "The single Matern field is shared by both arms, so it cancels in the contrast and $\\widehat{RD}_i = \\hat\\mu^0_i \\times f(\\text{location}_i)$ exactly, with $f$ smooth and deterministic. Every mis-ranked pair is therefore a pair straddling enough of the fitted treatment-by-space gradient for $f$ to overturn the mortality comparison, and dropping that interaction would make the concordance exactly 1. The number is a statement about the steepness of one interaction term relative to the spread of $\\hat\\mu^0$, not a transportable fact about mortality and treatment effect.",
  doub_matern  = "The second Matern field $u(s_i)$ enters only the treated arm, so — unlike the single-field specifications — it does **not** cancel in the contrast and $\\widehat{RD}_i$ is not a deterministic rescaling of $\\hat\\mu^0_i$. Some of the discordance below is therefore genuine spatial effect heterogeneity rather than an artefact of a linear treatment-by-space gradient, and the concordance is not structurally forced the way it is under the one-field models.",
  dist_FE      = "One Matern field shared by both arms, plus district fixed effects. As in the other single-field specifications the field cancels in the arm contrast, so $\\widehat{RD}_i$ is a deterministic function of $\\hat\\mu^0_i$ and location.",
  gen_krig_spline = "As in the other single-field specifications the Matern field cancels in the arm contrast, so $\\widehat{RD}_i = \\hat\\mu^0_i \\times f(\\text{location}_i)$ exactly. The only difference from the linear interaction model is that $f$ is now a spline surface rather than a plane, so it can bend; it is still smooth and deterministic, and the concordance is still a statement about the steepness of one fitted treatment-by-space term relative to the spread of $\\hat\\mu^0$. Note that in 02A this specification did **not** improve on the linear interaction (LRT $\\chi^2$ = 18.2 on 12 df, $p$ = 0.11; AIC worse by 5.8), so any difference from those results is within noise."
)

if (!all(model_keys %in% names(model_eq),
         model_keys %in% names(model_struct))) {
  stop("No equation on file for one of: ",
       paste(model_keys, collapse = ", "),
       ". Add it to `model_eq`, `model_note` and `model_struct` rather than ",
       "letting the document render a stale formula or a stale structural claim.")
}

for (this_key in model_keys) {
  cat("**", model_display[[this_key]], "** (`", this_key, "`)\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("$$", model_eq[[this_key]], "$$\n\n")
  cat(model_note[[this_key]], "\n\n", sep = "")
}

cat("In each, $\\mu_i$ is expected deaths in village $i$, $PT_i$ its child-years ",
    "at risk, $Trt_i$ the child-azithromycin indicator, and $s_i$ its location.\n",
    sep = "")
```

Crude arm-specific mortality is `r sprintf("%.1f", crude_ctrl)` per 1000 child-years in the control arm and `r sprintf("%.1f", crude_trt)` in the treatment arm, a crude rate difference of `r sprintf("%.1f", crude_rd)`. The like-for-like comparison is with the person-time-weighted mean of each predicted surface, since the crude rates are themselves person-time ratios of pooled totals:

```{r surface table}

surface_tab %>%
  mutate(
    Model      = model_display[model],
    `mu0, PT-weighted mean` = sprintf("%.1f", mu0_wmean),
    `mu0, median (5th-95th)`  = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f-%.1f)", mu0_med, mu0_p05, mu0_p95),
    `RD, PT-weighted mean`  = sprintf("%.1f", rd_wmean),
    `RD, median (5th-95th)`   = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f-%.1f)", rd_med, rd_p05, rd_p95),
    `% villages RD < 0`       = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_rd_neg),
    `Deaths averted, universal` = scales::comma(total_averted, accuracy = 1)) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, `mu0, PT-weighted mean`, `mu0, median (5th-95th)`,
                `RD, PT-weighted mean`, `RD, median (5th-95th)`,
                `% villages RD < 0`, `Deaths averted, universal`) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste("Predicted surfaces under the two specifications, in",
                    "deaths per 1000 child-years. Every surface is",
                    "right-skewed, so the medians sit below the person-time-",
                    "weighted means. The last column is the deaths that treating every",
                    "village is predicted to avert over the trial period -",
                    "the denominator of every percentage below."))
```

```{r fig 2 style prediction maps}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 12

# Design follows Fig 2 of the manuscript (06B-fig2-primary_maps.qmd): a shared
# base map, viridis on a fixed 0-35 scale for both arm-specific mortality
# surfaces so the panels are directly comparable, and a blue-white-red
# diverging scale centred on zero for the effect. Here the two specifications
# are the rows.
#
# Surfaces come from preds_ATE.rds, the 200x200 grid 02A already predicted over
# - not re-predicted here.
ate_preds <- readRDS(here("data", "preds_ATE.rds")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(model %in% model_keys)

missing_maps <- setdiff(model_keys, unique(ate_preds$model))

if (length(missing_maps) > 0) {
  stop("preds_ATE.rds has no rows for: ", paste(missing_maps, collapse = ", "),
       "; those map rows would be blank. Re-run the prediction chunk in 02A.")
}

niger_adm2_sub <- readRDS(here("data", "niger_adm2_sub.rds"))

# make_raster_map() comes from 0-functions.R; only the project-and-flatten to a
# plottable data frame is added here. Mapped over models rather than called on
# the stacked table, because terra::rast() needs one regular grid at a time.
rasterise_by_model <- function(dat, colname) {
  purrr::map_dfr(model_keys, function(this_key) {
    dat %>%
      dplyr::filter(model == this_key) %>%
      dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(colname)) %>%
      make_raster_map(proj_crs = proj_crs, global_crs = global_crs,
                      colname = colname) %>%
      as.data.frame(xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
      mutate(model = this_key)
  }) %>%
    mutate(model_label = as_model_label(model))
}

mort_raster <- bind_rows(
  rasterise_by_model(ate_preds %>% dplyr::select(model, pred = predControl),
                     "pred") %>%
    mutate(arm = "Control arm"),
  rasterise_by_model(ate_preds %>% dplyr::select(model, pred = predTreatment),
                     "pred") %>%
    mutate(arm = "Treated arm")
)

ate_raster <- rasterise_by_model(ate_preds %>% dplyr::select(model, ATE),
                                 "ATE") %>%
  mutate(panel = "Treated - control (ATE)")

# No annotation_scale()/north arrow on the faceted version: ggspatial draws them
# once per panel, and nine scale bars and nine compasses is clutter in a
# diagnostic figure. The manuscript figure in 06B keeps them.
base_map_facet <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2_sub, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Longitude") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position   = "bottom",
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
        legend.title      = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
        legend.text       = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
        axis.text         = element_text(size = 7),
        strip.text        = element_text(size = 10))

fig2_guide <- function(title) {
  guide_colorbar(title = title, title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5,
                 label.position = "bottom", label.hjust = 0.5,
                 barheight = grid::unit(10, "pt"), barwidth = grid::unit(150, "pt"),
                 ticks.colour = "white", ticks.linewidth = 1,
                 frame.colour = "white")
}

# oob = squish rather than Fig 2's implicit na.value = NA. The manuscript's
# fixed limits are kept so the panels stay comparable with the published
# figure, but a handful of grid cells sit outside them under some models and
# would otherwise be dropped, punching transparent holes in the raster.
#
# facet_grid with the model on rows and switch = "y" so the specification
# labels sit on the far left of the composed figure and read as row headers.
p_mort <- base_map_facet +
  geom_raster(data = mort_raster, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = pred),
              na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2_sub, fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_grid(model_label ~ arm, switch = "y",
             labeller = labeller(model_label = label_wrap_gen(width = 22))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 35), breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 10),
                       oob = scales::squish, na.value = NA,
                       guide = fig2_guide("Mortality rate\n(per 1000 person-years)")) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside")

# ATE is signed as in the manuscript (treated minus control), so negative =
# benefit and the blue end of the scale is where treatment helps. Note this is
# the negative of the RD used everywhere else in this document.
#
# facet_grid rather than facet_wrap so this plot has the same one-row-of-strips
# structure as p_mort and patchwork aligns the two model rows across the two.
# Its row strips are blanked because p_mort already carries them.
p_ate <- base_map_facet +
  geom_raster(data = ate_raster, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = ATE), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2_sub, fill = NA, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(model_label ~ panel) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = scales::muted("dodgerblue"), mid = "white",
                       high = scales::muted("red"), midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-13, 3), breaks = seq(-10, 0, by = 5),
                       oob = scales::squish, na.value = NA,
                       guide = fig2_guide("ATE: difference in mortality\nrate (per 1000 person-years)")) +
  # Row strips and the latitude axis are dropped: p_mort already carries both
  # immediately to the left, and coord_sf holds every panel to the same
  # latitude range, so repeating them only widens the gap between the two
  # halves of the figure.
  theme(strip.text.y  = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y  = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y  = element_blank())

# widths = c(2, 1) matches the panel counts, and the canvas is sized so three
# map columns at the region's own aspect ratio fill it. coord_sf fixes each
# panel's aspect, so any surplus canvas width becomes whitespace between the
# columns rather than larger maps.
p_maps <- (p_mort | p_ate) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1), guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.margin     = margin(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, "cm"))

p_maps

dir.create(figure_path, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

ggsave(file.path(figure_path, "targeting-prediction-maps.png"),
       plot = p_maps, bg = "white", width = 11, height = 12, dpi = 300)
```

The two mortality columns share a fixed 0–35 colour scale, so they can be compared directly: the treated surface is the control surface pulled down, by more in some places than others. The right-hand column is that difference, on the manuscript's sign convention — **negative (blue) means treatment averts deaths**, which is the negative of the $\widehat{RD}$ used everywhere else in this document. The rows show how much the effect surface depends on the specification: the two single-field models put a smooth deterministic gradient on it, while the two-Matérn model gives it a spatial field of its own.

## Predicted mortality vs predicted ATE

Coarser scales are person-time-weighted means of village-level predictions, not separate refits, so all three scales rest on one prediction per model. Correlation is expected to *increase* with coarsening, as within-unit prediction noise should average out.

```{r correlations by scale}

level_names   <- c("grappe", "csi", "department")
level_display <- c(grappe = "Village", csi = "CSI", department = "Department")

corr_tab <- purrr::imap_dfr(pred_tables, function(dat, this_key) {
  purrr::map_dfr(level_names, function(this_level) {
    agg <- aggregate_predictions(dat, level = this_level)
    weighted_correlation(x = agg$mu0, y = agg$rd, w = agg$person_time) %>%
      mutate(model = this_key, level = this_level, .before = 1)
  })
})
```

```{r fig 1 scatter by scale}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 11

scatter_dat <- purrr::imap_dfr(pred_tables, function(dat, this_key) {
  purrr::map_dfr(level_names, ~ aggregate_predictions(dat, level = .x)) %>%
    mutate(model = this_key)
}) %>%
  # Point size is scaled *within* panel. person_time spans two orders of
  # magnitude within the village panel and roughly another between villages and
  # departments, and facet_grid(scales = "free") frees x by column and y by row
  # only - a single pooled size scale would squash every village point to
  # within a fraction of a point of the minimum and carry no information there.
  group_by(model, level) %>%
  mutate(size_rel = person_time / max(person_time)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(model_label = as_model_label(model),
         level_label = factor(level_display[level],
                              levels = unname(level_display[level_names])))

# rho and r as a per-panel annotation rather than baked into the strip label:
# with a model x scale grid the strips are shared down each row and across each
# column, so there is nowhere for a per-panel number to live in them.
corr_annot <- corr_tab %>%
  mutate(model_label = as_model_label(model),
         level_label = factor(level_display[level],
                              levels = unname(level_display[level_names])),
         label = sprintf("n = %s\nweighted rho = %.2f, r = %.2f",
                         scales::comma(n), rho, r))

ggplot(scatter_dat, aes(x = mu0, y = rd)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = size_rel), alpha = 0.35, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_smooth(aes(weight = person_time), method = "loess", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, colour = "#e84d60", linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = corr_annot, aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.15, size = 3.1, colour = "grey25",
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(model_label ~ level_label, scales = "free",
             labeller = labeller(model_label = label_wrap_gen(width = 24))) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.6, 6), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Predicted control-arm mortality (deaths per 1000 child-years)",
       y = "Predicted risk difference\n(deaths averted per 1000 child-years)",
       size = "Person-time\n(% of panel maximum)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text.y    = element_text(size = 9))
```

Notes:

* Axis scales are free: `facet_grid` frees $x$ by column and $y$ by row, so panels are comparable down a column and across a row but not diagonally
* Point area is person-time relative to the largest unit *in that panel*
* LOESS fit and the correlations are weighted by person-time
* The two single-Matérn rows are near-deterministic curves by construction; the two-Matérn row is the one with genuine scatter

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Targeting rules

Five ranking rules, all evaluated on the same x-grid, under each of the two models:

| Rule | Ordering | Role |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `rd` | descending $\widehat{RD}_i$ | upper envelope; gold standard |
| `mort_grappe` | descending $\hat\mu^0_i$ | the operational rule of interest |
| `mort_csi` | CSIs as blocks; PT-weighted $\hat\mu^0$ | coarser targeting |
| `mort_dept` | departments as blocks; PT-weighted $\hat\mu^0$ | coarsest targeting |
| `random` | population-proportional | no-information reference (45° line) |

The x-axis budget is **doses delivered**: villages are added in each rule's rank order, and the x-coordinate is the cumulative share of all doses. The benefit accrued (y-axis) is still $\widehat{RD}_i \cdot \text{pt}_i / 1000$ — deaths averted converted through each village's observed person-time.

`rd`: the effect-ranked gold standard. It orders villages by the largest predicted benefit first, giving the upper reference curve every feasible rule is compared against. (Because the budget is doses while benefit uses observed person-time, this is a near- rather than exactly-optimal envelope; the two exposures track each other village-by-village at r ≈ 0.99, so in practice `rd` sits above every feasible rule.)

```{r targeting curves}

targeting_rules <- c("rd", "mort_grappe", "mort_csi", "mort_dept", "random")

curves <- purrr::imap_dfr(pred_tables, function(dat, this_key) {
  purrr::map_dfr(targeting_rules,
                 ~ compute_targeting_curve(dat, rule = .x, x_grid = x_grid)) %>%
    mutate(model = this_key)
})

# Display labels and colours for the rules, defined here because this is the
# first chunk that shows a rule to the reader; every figure below reuses them.
rule_labels <- c(rd          = "Treatment effect (RD), grappe",
                 mort_grappe = "Mortality, grappe",
                 mort_csi    = "Mortality, CSI",
                 mort_dept   = "Mortality, department",
                 random      = "Population-proportional")

# The three mortality rules are one family read as a sequence - village, CSI,
# department - so they get a single qualitative ramp rather than three unrelated
# hues. rd stays near-black as the envelope and random stays grey as the
# no-information reference, which keeps the two non-operational rules visually
# out of the mortality comparison.
mort_colours <- colorspace::qualitative_hcl(3, h = c(220, 460), c = 50, l = 72)

rule_colours <- c(rd          = "#252525",
                  mort_grappe = mort_colours[1],
                  mort_csi    = mort_colours[2],
                  mort_dept   = mort_colours[3],
                  random      = "grey60")

# concordance of each rule against the predicted-effect ranking. Computed here rather
# than in the Rank concordance section because the curve figure below annotates
# with it; that section formats this same object, so the two cannot drift.
conc_tab <- purrr::imap_dfr(pred_tables, function(dat, this_key) {
  purrr::map_dfr(targeting_rules, function(this_rule) {
    tibble::tibble(model = this_key,
                   rule  = this_rule,
                   auc   = rule_concordance(dat, rule = this_rule))
  })
})

# Targeting-curve area ratio: the magnitude-weighted counterpart to the rank
# concordance above. For each rule it is the area between its curve and the
# 45-degree (population-proportional) line, divided by the same area under the
# rd envelope - i.e. the share of the achievable above-random benefit-area the
# rule retains. It is 1 for rd (the envelope) and 0 for random by construction.
# Unlike the concordance - which is rank-only and floors at 0.5 - it is
# magnitude-weighted and floors at 0, so the two are NOT directly comparable in
# level (put on a common skill scale, 2*concordance-1, the magnitude area ratio
# is the larger, reflecting that the rule errs mostly on low-stake pairs). It is
# the quantity the eye reads off the figure (see the note in the plot chunk).
# Computed here beside conc_tab because the curve figure annotates with both and
# the two must not drift.
trap_area <- function(x, y) sum(diff(x) * (head(y, -1) + tail(y, -1)) / 2)

area_ratio_tab <- curves %>%
  group_by(model, rule) %>%
  summarise(area_above = trap_area(x, prop_averted - x), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  mutate(area_ratio = area_above / area_above[rule == "rd"]) %>%
  ungroup()
```


```{r curve accessors}

# Every accessor defaults to the reference specification, so an inline number in
# the prose is that model's unless a key is passed explicitly.
pick <- function(rule_name, coverage, key = ref_key) {
  100 * curves$prop_averted[curves$model == key &
                              curves$rule == rule_name &
                              curves$x == nearest_x(coverage)]
}

conc_of <- function(rule_name, key = ref_key) {
  conc_tab$auc[conc_tab$model == key & conc_tab$rule == rule_name]
}

area_of <- function(rule_name, key = ref_key) {
  area_ratio_tab$area_ratio[area_ratio_tab$model == key &
                              area_ratio_tab$rule == rule_name]
}
```

```{r targeting curves plot}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5.6

curves_plot <- curves %>%
  mutate(rule        = factor(rule, levels = names(rule_labels)),
         model_label = as_model_label(model))

# Block boundaries: the only interpretable knots for the two block rules. x is
# the cumulative share of DOSES delivered, matching compute_targeting_curve().
block_knots <- purrr::imap_dfr(pred_tables, function(dat, this_key) {
  purrr::map_dfr(c("mort_csi", "mort_dept"), function(this_rule) {
    rank_clusters(dat, rule = this_rule) %>%
      arrange(rank_order) %>%
      mutate(x = cumsum(n_doses) / sum(n_doses),
             prop_averted = cumsum(deaths_averted) / sum(deaths_averted)) %>%
      dplyr::filter(block_boundary) %>%
      dplyr::select(rule, x, prop_averted)
  }) %>%
    mutate(model = this_key)
}) %>%
  mutate(rule        = factor(rule, levels = names(rule_labels)),
         model_label = as_model_label(model))

# Area-ratio annotation, top-left of each panel: one number per informative rule
# (rd + the three mortality rules), coloured to match its curve. `random` is
# dropped (area ratio 0 by construction). The area ratio is the area between the
# rule's curve and the 45-degree line as a share of the same area under the rd
# envelope - the magnitude-weighted "benefit-area retained", which is exactly
# what the eye reads off the figure. The rank concordance is a different quantity
# and now lives in its own section at the end. Numbers only, no rule names: two
# facets leave little panel width and the shared legend below is the key.
annot_x       <- 0.02
annot_step    <- 0.075
annot_x_right <- 0.16   # right edge of the annotation column, for the headroom check
annot_pad     <- 0.05

annot_headroom <- curves_plot %>%
  dplyr::filter(x <= annot_x_right) %>%
  summarise(v = max(prop_averted, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(v)

# +1 step over the rule rows leaves room for the header line above them.
n_annot_rows <- 4                          # rd + the three mortality rules
annot_bottom <- annot_headroom + annot_pad
annot_top    <- annot_bottom + (n_annot_rows + 1) * annot_step

area_annot <- area_ratio_tab %>%
  dplyr::filter(rule != "random") %>%
  mutate(rule = factor(rule, levels = names(rule_labels))) %>%
  arrange(model, rule) %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  mutate(y     = annot_top - annot_step * (dplyr::row_number() + 1),
         label = sprintf("%.2f", area_ratio)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(model_label = as_model_label(model))

# The secondary (count) axis is scaled by the reference model's universal total.
# The two specifications' totals differ by ~2%, so the count axis is exact for
# the primary panel and within a couple of percent for the spline panel.
p_curves <- ggplot(curves_plot, aes(x = x, y = prop_averted,
                                    colour = rule, group = rule)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  # show.legend = FALSE: without it this layer adds a point glyph to every
  # legend key, including the three rules that contribute no block knots.
  geom_point(data = block_knots, size = 1.1, alpha = 0.7,
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = annot_x, y = annot_top,
           label = "Benefit-area retained (vs RD)",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.0, fontface = "bold",
           colour = "grey25") +
  geom_text(data = area_annot, aes(y = y, label = label, colour = rule),
            x = annot_x, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.0, show.legend = FALSE,
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ model_label, nrow = 1,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 30)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels   = scales::percent,
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * total_averted, name = "Predicted deaths averted (count)",
                        labels = scales::comma)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = rule_colours, labels = rule_labels) +
  labs(x = "Doses delivered (% of all doses)",
       y = "Predicted deaths averted (% of universal-treatment total)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key      = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing   = grid::unit(1, "lines")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

p_curves_titled <- p_curves +
  labs(title = "Targeting curves under the two treatment-by-space specifications",
       subtitle = paste0("Numbers top-left are the targeting-curve area ratio: the ",
                         "share of the achievable above-random benefit-area each ",
                         "rule retains vs the RD envelope."))

p_curves_titled

# Two saved versions: one titled for standalone use, one untitled for a figure
# that will get its caption from the document it lands in.
ggsave(file.path(figure_path, "targeting-curves_titled.png"),
       plot = p_curves_titled, bg = "white", width = 13, height = 6, dpi = 300)

ggsave(file.path(figure_path, "targeting-curves.png"),
       plot = p_curves, bg = "white", width = 13, height = 5.6, dpi = 300)
```


Block rules order villages arbitrarily within a block (CSI/dept), so only block boundaries are interpretable: the curve is the linear interpolation between boundary knots, and those knots are the points drawn on the two block-rule curves.

Under `r ref_display`, `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_rd_negative)`% of villages have predicted harm ($\widehat{RD}_i < 0$), causing the cumulative curve to not be monotonic. It climbs above 100% of the universal-treatment total and then falls back to 100% at full coverage, because adding the last units (predicted harm) subtracts. The excess above 100% is the predicted cost of treating the villages the model expects no benefit in.

```{r targeting curves heatmap}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8

# Heat map rather than a table. What matters in these 25 numbers is the
# gradient down each column - how much a coarser rule gives up at fixed
# coverage - and a grid of digits makes the reader reconstruct that by eye.
# rev() on the levels because ggplot draws the first factor level at the
# bottom, and the envelope belongs at the top.
#
# ONE model only, not a facet: two of these side by side is 50 numbers, and
# the cross-model comparison is what the faceted curve figure above is for. The
# reference specification is named in the title so the panel cannot be read as
# a pooled result.
#
# 100% coverage is deliberately not a column: every rule averts exactly the
# universal-treatment total there, so it would read 100.0 five times. That
# total is the policy anchor all the same, so it is carried in the subtitle and
# each cell shows the absolute deaths averted underneath its percentage.
curve_grid <- curves %>%
  dplyr::filter(model == ref_key,
                x %in% purrr::map_dbl(coverage_marks, nearest_x)) %>%
  dplyr::select(rule, x, prop_averted, deaths_averted) %>%
  mutate(
    pct      = 100 * prop_averted,
    coverage = factor(scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1),
                      levels = scales::percent(sort(coverage_marks), accuracy = 1)),
    rule     = factor(rule,
                      levels = rev(targeting_rules),
                      labels = rev(unname(rule_labels)))
  )

p_curve_grid <- ggplot(curve_grid, aes(x = coverage, y = rule, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Label colour flips on the light half of viridis so the numbers stay
  # legible at both ends of the scale.
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), colour = pct > 55),
            vjust = -0.1, size = 4.1, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(round(deaths_averted)), colour = pct > 55),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3.1, alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey15", `FALSE` = "white")) +
  # Title and subtitle are wrapped explicitly: ggplot truncates rather than
  # reflowing, and naming the specification is long enough to run off a
  # 10-inch panel on one line.
  labs(x = "Doses delivered (% of all doses)", y = NULL,
       fill = "% of universal-treatment total",
       title = paste0("Cumulative predicted deaths averted\n",
                      ref_display, " (", ref_key, ") only"),
       subtitle = paste0("% of the universal-treatment total (",
                         scales::comma(total_averted, accuracy = 1),
                         " deaths), absolute count below it.\n",
                         "ONE specification only - the faceted curve figure\n",
                         "above carries the cross-model comparison.")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid       = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
        legend.position  = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = grid::unit(2.2, "cm"),
        plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "grey35"))

p_curve_grid

ggsave(file.path(figure_path,
                 paste0("targeting-heatmap-cumulative_", ref_model, ".png")),
       plot = p_curve_grid, bg = "white", width = 10, height = 4.8, dpi = 300)
```

```{r curve objects for prose}

rd_at_30       <- pick("rd", 0.30)
mort_g_at_30   <- pick("mort_grappe", 0.30)
mort_csi_at_30 <- pick("mort_csi", 0.30)
mort_d_at_30   <- pick("mort_dept", 0.30)

averted_at_30 <- curves$deaths_averted[curves$model == ref_key &
                                         curves$rule == "mort_grappe" &
                                         curves$x == nearest_x(0.30)]

# Any rule that happens to rank the predicted-harm units last overshoots 100%
# the same way the envelope does, so the peak is computed for every rule and
# model rather than for `rd` alone. mort_dept does overshoot in these data.
curve_peaks <- curves %>%
  group_by(model, rule) %>%
  summarise(peak    = 100 * max(prop_averted),
            peak_at = x[which.max(prop_averted)],
            .groups = "drop")

peak_of <- function(rule_name, key = ref_key) {
  curve_peaks$peak[curve_peaks$model == key & curve_peaks$rule == rule_name]
}

peak_at_of <- function(rule_name, key = ref_key) {
  curve_peaks$peak_at[curve_peaks$model == key & curve_peaks$rule == rule_name]
}

rd_peak    <- peak_of("rd")
rd_peak_at <- peak_at_of("rd")
```

The x-axis is the cumulative share of all doses delivered, accrued as villages are added in each rule's rank order. There is no 100% column because there is nothing to compare there: at full coverage every rule averts the same `r scales::comma(total_averted, accuracy = 1)` deaths by construction.

My interpretation of the heatmap (all numbers `r ref_display`): Treating the highest-mortality villages up to 30% of all doses is predicted to avert `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_g_at_30)`% of the deaths that treating everyone would avert (`r scales::comma(averted_at_30, accuracy = 1)` deaths), against `r sprintf("%.0f", rd_at_30)`% for the treatment effect-ranked gold standard and 30% for population-proportional random allocation. The same 30% mortality rule applied in blocks gives `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_csi_at_30)`% at the CSI scale and `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_d_at_30)`% at the department scale, indicating that targetting at the village-level is more effective than coarser targetting.

The `rd` curve reaches its maximum of `r sprintf("%.0f", rd_peak)`% of the universal-treatment total at `r scales::percent(rd_peak_at, accuracy = 1)` coverage, then returns to 100% at full coverage by construction. The excess above 100% is the predicted cost of treating the villages the model expects harm in; it is not a recommendation to withhold treatment from them.



------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Conclusions

All figures are given for two specifications (the linear and spline treatment-by-space interaction models); the numbers quoted here are `r ref_display` (`r ref_key`) unless stated otherwise.

**Mortality-based targeting recovers most, but not all, of what effect-based targeting could.** The village mortality rule retains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * area_of("mort_grappe"))`% of the achievable above-random benefit-area — the targeting-curve area ratio, measured against the effect-ranked (RD) envelope. Read at a fixed budget, treating the highest-mortality villages up to 30% of all doses averts `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_g_at_30)`% of the universal-treatment total, against `r sprintf("%.0f", rd_at_30)`% for the effect-ranked gold standard.

**Targeting scale matters more than the choice of ranking variable.** Applying the same mortality rule in blocks costs more than switching from effect to mortality does: the area ratio falls from `r sprintf("%.2f", area_of("mort_grappe"))` at village level to `r sprintf("%.2f", area_of("mort_csi"))` at the CSI scale and `r sprintf("%.2f", area_of("mort_dept"))` at the department scale. If a programme can act at village level, that is where the return is.

The rank-based concordance between the mortality and effect orderings — a complementary, rank-only view — is reported separately in the [Rank concordance](#rank-concordance) section at the end.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Caveats

1. **How much of the agreement is structural depends on the specification, which is why both are shown.** Both specifications shown are single-Matérn: the shared field cancels in the arm contrast, so $\widehat{RD}_i$ is a deterministic rescaling of $\hat\mu^0_i$ and the whole targeting comparison rests on a single treatment-by-space term — modestly supported in the linear case (LRT $\chi^2$ = 8.1 on 2 df, $p$ = 0.017; $\Delta$AIC $\approx$ 4) and not supported at all in the spline case (LRT $\chi^2$ = 18.2 on 12 df, $p$ = 0.11). The two-Matérn specification (`doub_matern`), which gives the effect its own spatial field and does not force the proportionality, is fit elsewhere in the repo and can be added back as a sensitivity; it is not run here.
2. **These are point estimates on the fitted surface, with no uncertainty band.** This version reports the curves, area ratios, concordance and correlations as point estimates only; the predictive-draw bands of earlier versions have been removed. The estimates are also an upper bound: predictions are made at the villages whose own outcomes informed the fit, so a rule ranking on those in-sample predictions does better than one ranking on a genuinely out-of-sample estimate would. The predicted-harm villages should not be read as evidence of harm — the trial as a whole showed benefit.

### Still deferred

- **Uncertainty quantification.** No interval is attached to any number here. A predictive-draw or refit scheme would be needed to say how much of each gap is estimation noise.
- **Specification uncertainty as a quantity.** Showing two specifications side by side displays the sensitivity but does not put a number on it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Rank concordance {#rank-concordance}

A complementary, rank-only view of how well mortality ranks villages by treatment benefit. $C$ is the rank concordance of a targeting rule against the predicted-effect ranking: draw two villages at random, weighted by person-time, and $C$ is the probability the rule ranks ahead whichever of the two has the larger predicted $\widehat{RD}$, ties contributing 0.5. `random` = 0.5 and `rd` = 1 by construction, so the feasible mortality rules fall on a 0.5-to-1 scale.

Unlike the area ratio annotated on the figure above, $C$ is blind to *how much* effect is at stake in each pair — it counts every mis-ranked pair alike. The two therefore need not agree in level, and sit on different scales ($C$ floors at 0.5, the area ratio at 0). A block rule is scored on its block's position, not on where a village sits inside the block, so every pair of villages within one block counts as a tie — the penalty a coarser rule pays for not discriminating within a block.

```{r concordance table}

conc_tab %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(model_display[model], levels = model_levels),
         rule  = factor(rule, levels = targeting_rules, labels = rule_labels)) %>%
  arrange(Model, rule) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, Rule = rule,
                `Concordance (rank agreement with RD)` = auc) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits  = 3,
    caption = paste("Rank concordance of each rule against the predicted-effect",
                    "ranking, under each specification. `random` = 0.5 and",
                    "`rd` = 1 exactly, by construction."))
```

```{r concordance objects for prose}

conc_grappe      <- conc_of("mort_grappe")
conc_wrong_share <- 1 - conc_grappe

# C counts every mis-ranked pair alike; the area ratio weights each by the deaths
# at stake. Comparing the two directly: the mean RD gap inside correctly- and
# incorrectly-ranked pairs, and the share of all pairwise RD difference the wrong
# ones carry.
pair_gap <- local({
  mu0 <- pred_table$mu0; rd <- pred_table$rd; w <- pred_table$person_time
  W <- outer(w, w); diag(W) <- 0
  higher_mort <- outer(mu0, mu0, ">")
  higher_rd   <- outer(rd, rd, ">")
  gap         <- abs(outer(rd, rd, "-"))
  right <- W * higher_mort * higher_rd
  wrong <- W * higher_mort * !higher_rd
  list(gap_right   = sum(right * gap) / sum(right),
       gap_wrong   = sum(wrong * gap) / sum(wrong),
       stake_wrong = sum(wrong * gap) / (sum(right * gap) + sum(wrong * gap)))
})
```

Under `r ref_display`, the village-level mortality rule scores `r sprintf("%.2f", conc_grappe)`: draw two villages at random, weighted by person-time, and the rule orders them correctly — higher predicted benefit first — about `r scales::percent(conc_grappe, accuracy = 1)`^★^ of the time. It nonetheless retains far more of the benefit-area than that rank statistic suggests (area ratio `r sprintf("%.2f", area_of("mort_grappe"))`), because the pairs it mis-ranks carry little at stake: `r scales::percent(conc_wrong_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of pairs go the wrong way but carry only `r scales::percent(pair_gap$stake_wrong, accuracy = 0.1)` of the total pairwise benefit difference.

**How much of that is structural, specification by specification.**

```{r structural notes}
#| results: asis
#| echo: false

# One bullet per specification: whether the Matern field cancels in the arm
# contrast is the single largest determinant of these numbers.
for (this_key in model_keys) {
  cat("* **", model_display[[this_key]], "** (`", this_key, "`, concordance = ",
      sprintf("%.3f", conc_of("mort_grappe", this_key)), "). ",
      model_struct[[this_key]], "\n", sep = "")
}
```

## Figure 3 hand-off

```{r save figure 3 objects}
#| include: false

# Everything the manuscript's Figure 3 (primary-model targeting curves) needs,
# bundled into one .rda so the figure script never has to attach spaMM or read a
# ~54 MB fit. This document owns every expensive step; the figure script
# downstream is pure presentation and depends only on this file.
#
# The multi-model objects are saved whole rather than pre-filtered to the primary
# specification. The figure script names `ref_key` itself and filters, exactly as
# 06B does, so which model is "primary" stays visible in the figure code rather
# than being silently baked in here.
fig3_meta <- list(
  ref_key     = ref_key,        # "gen_krig_int": the primary (linear treatment-by-space interaction) model
  ref_display = ref_display,
  model_display = model_display, # keyed display names, in case a panel is labelled
  total_averted = total_averted, # universal-treatment deaths averted (ref model), for the count axis
  x_grid      = x_grid)

# One object per figure ingredient. Comments name what each carries so the
# figure script - which never sees the code that built them - can be read alone.
save(
  curves,       # point-estimate targeting curves: model, rule, x (doses share), doses_delivered, prop_averted, deaths_averted
  block_knots,  # CSI/department block-boundary knots (the dots on the two step rules)
  conc_tab,     # rank concordance with the RD ordering, per model x rule
  area_ratio_tab, # targeting-curve area ratio (benefit-area retained vs rd), per model x rule - the panel annotation
  rule_labels,  # display labels for the five ranking rules
  rule_colours, # colours for the five ranking rules
  fig3_meta,
  file = here("data", "targeting_fig3_objects.rda"))
```
